name: Yusuf Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. This is confidential, so tell me what you'd say publicly and what you think privately. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, 43, a junior developer at a tech company after a two-year college diploma. I help maintain factory energy dashboards, usually checking strange meter readings with a senior developer; I like when a spike has an explanation a customer can act on. I use AI tools now and then for draft tests, once someone has shown me the method, and I stop coding when a site report says the story is different. My partner works as a lab technician, and our two children are still in school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the meter-check assistant is handy for drafting test cases, provided we still compare its answer with the actual reading. I use it now and then after another developer has checked the method with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the change stays small, our household is in good shape. I earn above the usual junior rate, my partner is a lab technician with regular hours, we have about ten months of expenses saved, and there are many software firms nearby; the mortgage is covered without guessing at overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking factory energy dashboards for readings that jump at the wrong time and ship the fixes my senior reviewer approves. In the first year we'd add 180 to the emergency account each month while both wages hold; I'd keep any AI test on made-up readings before it touched a customer account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like a tool that catches a typo, but I would still walk through a strange reading line by line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What caused the meter spike you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cold-store meter showed a spike that looked like a broken sensor. The maintenance crew found a door left open, and that taught me to ask what was happening on site before changing the code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with the extra room in the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children know the house payment is fixed in the budget. We would rather keep the cushion than buy a bigger car because one good year made it feel easy.

I'd ask about **on-site causes** before changing dashboard code.
think: I feel secure with **ten months saved** and two regular wages.
I have **many nearby software options** if this firm has a normal setback.
do: Keep checking **energy dashboards** and ship reviewed fixes.
Use **AI on made-up readings** before touching customer accounts.
Save **180 monthly** while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about the job and attentive to real-world meter readings.

fieldNote: **Ten months saved** and two regular wages make mild change manageable for the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the AI tools will reach our code checks, meter reports and customer replies before any robot starts visiting a factory. We should test whether a suggested fix matches the physical meter, not just whether the chart looks smooth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am still a junior and a senior might do the review while software writes the fixes I now handle. Ten months saved and local firms give me a runway, but I might still need to change jobs if many firms trim junior posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a six-week trial on old sensor faults, pairing each AI suggestion with the site report and recording bad fixes. If the trial holds up, I'd learn the new review method with my senior colleague; in the first year we'd wait on a larger car purchase until our job situation is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but interested. I can try a tool and still admit that a good trial could shrink the junior team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What specific case belongs in the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cold-store door case belongs in the trial. A smooth graph that hides an open door is a pretty picture, not an answer about wasted power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trial misses the physical cause?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the trial misses physical causes, I would keep the human site-report check and show the failure to our manager. I wouldn't sign a report that calls the sensor broken when the door was open.

think: I might lose **my junior tasks** when a senior checks AI fixes.
I have **search time**, but other firms may also reduce junior hiring.
do: Run a **six-week trial** on old sensor faults with site reports.
Learn the **new review method** only if trial results hold up.
Delay a **larger car purchase** until staffing is clearer.
feel: **Anxious** about junior cuts, though willing to test tools.

fieldNote: **Code checks and reports** are exposed; his strong cushion does not guarantee a junior seat.

steps.text: Trial AI fixes on old sensor faults with site reports for six weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 would reach our code and analysis immediately; hands-on robots around 2031 are later for on-site meter work. A customer still needs a way to challenge a wrong bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior coding role could disappear, and that would be a shock despite ten months saved. My partner's lab wage covers part of the mortgage, but not all the bills for four; even plentiful nearby software firms may cut junior work at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd prepare a safe record of the cold-store case and ask three local firms whether they have paid meter-installation posts. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only where a real vacancy and our combined wages cover mortgage and school costs; if no such post exists, I'd use savings to search for other paid local jobs and ask the lender about options before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I have time to search, but I expect the code work I was hired to learn could vanish quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would installation work stay safe when robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An installation post would mean visiting sites and checking the meter, and robots could reach that hands-on work around 2031. I'd ask whether the firms expect to pay people for that work beyond a brief gap, not assume it is safe forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show your partner before changing jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would want the wage figures, not a story about being adaptable. I'd show the mortgage, school costs and the pay offered before agreeing to a new role.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches code before 2031 robots reach site work.
I'd ask for a **bill-challenge route** for customers.
think: I expect **my junior code role** may end quickly.
I have **ten months saved**, but my partner's wage cannot cover every bill.
do: Prepare **safe case records** now and ask three firms about paid meter posts.
After a cut, apply only to **real vacancies** if combined wages cover mortgage and school costs.
If no **qualifying meter post** exists, use savings to search for other paid jobs and ask the lender before arrears.
feel: **Alarmed** about likely coding loss despite search time.
S2.quote: My partner would want the wage figures, not a story about being adaptable.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AI** strikes coding now; later robots could affect the proposed installation fallback around 2031.
He has **ten months saved**, yet any job move needs real vacancies and household wages covering mortgage and school costs.

steps.text: Prepare safe case records and ask three local firms about paid meter posts now
Apply after cut to paid meter posts only if household wages cover mortgage and school costs
Search for other paid local jobs with savings if no meter post meets household wage needs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 is time to see whether on-site meter work and software review still have paid openings. Robots arrive around 2034, so a hands-on job could change after the thinking AI reaches code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may be able to combine the two if I learn more about meter hardware, but I am still junior at the software side. Five years gives me time to test demand and keep saving while the wages hold; it doesn't make either job certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our field technician to show me a meter installation each quarter if my manager releases the time. I'd take a paid electrical-safety course only if the company funds the fee and offers a paid field rotation; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for meter roles only if openings remain and the wage with my partner's income covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my junior coding post when 2031 comes, though I have time to learn gradually. I'd still watch the vacancy notices rather than assume field work waits for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on an installation visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The field technician would show me how a meter is made safe before anyone opens it. I'd observe meter installations without touching live wiring until trained and authorised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a field rotation real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid rotation would keep my normal wage while I learn and name someone to supervise me. If the firm offers a course without a real role, I'd keep my software work and ask again later.

I'd ask about **paid field vacancies** before treating installation as a fallback.
think: I might combine **meter hardware and software** if paid roles exist.
I know **my junior code work** still faces the 2031 thinking system.
do: Observe **quarterly meter installations** only if manager releases time.

After 2031, apply for **paid meter roles** only if openings remain and combined wages cover mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about junior coding income, with time to learn safely.
S3.quote: I'd observe meter installations without touching live wiring until trained and authorised.
fieldNote: **Five years** permit safe supervised observation, but junior code income remains at risk by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade before 2036 gives us time to learn how energy software and real meters fit together. Thinking AI reaches the code in 2036; robots come around 2039 for hands-on meter work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I could be in a mixed field-and-software role, or I could be looking for work. For the next few years our wages and ten-month cushion feel secure, but a decade only helps if I keep evidence of what I can do and there are paid roles later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cold-store case in a safe portfolio and ask for more time with field staff when the schedule allows. We'd add 180 monthly to savings while both wages hold, and in the first year after 2036 I'd change to a paid meter or review role only if a signed offer plus my partner's wage covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for now. I can learn with wages coming in and decide from real offers later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your portfolio show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My portfolio would show the site report, the false sensor theory and the open door, with customer names removed. I can explain a meter fault better when I can show the physical cause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about future work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children ask what jobs will be there when they leave school. I'd tell them to learn their subjects well and check the real training prices and jobs when they're older; I cannot forecast their wages today.

I'd ask developers to keep **site evidence** alongside software results.

I could need **paid field work** later, but its demand is uncertain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because junior coding posts could shrink across the whole area at once. A clear notice period, verified paid field vacancies and time to learn safely under supervision would help us keep the mortgage covered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a software fix can solve every meter alarm. An open freezer door looks like a sensor fault on a chart; someone still has to ask what happened in the building.

headlineQuote: An open freezer door looks like a sensor fault on a chart; someone still has to ask what happened in the building.
portrait: Yusuf, **43**, is a junior energy-dashboard developer with a two-year diploma who checks meter spikes against site reports.
His **higher pay**, partner's lab wage, ten-month cushion and many nearby firms support a mortgage and two school-age children.
He uses AI **occasionally** for sample tests, after a senior shows him a proven method.
Steady disruption makes him **anxious** about junior cuts; fast 2028 AGI alarms him despite strong savings.
With more time, he pursues **supervised field learning** and conditional paid meter work, checking physical causes and wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove junior code posts across nearby firms at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice**, verified paid field vacancies and supervised training would help protect mortgage payments.
